newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbia's Telekom sale seen boosting Milosevic.
newsitem.headline: Serbia's Telekom sale seen boosting Milosevic.

text.p: The partial privatisation of Serbia's state-owned telecommunications company has given the Socialist government a financial boost ahead of presidential and parliamentary elections, political sources said on Friday.

The sale this month of a 49 percent stake in Telekom Srbija to Italian and Greek telecom companies Stet and OTE raised 1.568 billion German marks ($1.254 billion) of which 80 percent is already in the coffers of the Serbian Development Fund. The balance is to be paid in January 1998.
The fund said the money would be used to improve industrial output and provide loans for exporting industries.
But independent economists and diplomats said it might be used to defuse social tensions in the build-up to elections due by the end of the year rather than to develop viable programmes.

"The government has lost credibility and it is difficult to believe it will respect economic rather than political reasoning in the election year," said Dana Popovic, analyst at the private Centre for Economic Studies Ces Mekon.

"Social issues will be one of the factors in deciding the way the money is spent due to growing demands from workers, pensioners, health and education sectors for the payment of overdue wages," said Radovan Kovacevic, director of the Belgrade-based Institute for Foreign Trade.

A diplomat who declined to be named said: "I fear the funds could be directed more towards big state-run loss-making systems which employ the majority of the workforce and whose managers are also government ministers."

Although an outer wall of sanctions, limiting Serbia's access to international finance, has remained in place since U.N. sanctions were lifted in 1996, the telecommunications deal provides President Slobodan Milosevic with a lifeline.

Political sources said Western governments, disillusioned by the Serbian opposition's failure to build on successful anti-Milosevic street protests earlier this year, were swinging back to him as a source of regional stability.
"The West fears events like those in Albania could be repeated here which would lead to destabilisation of the entire Balkans," said Zarko Korac, an independent political analyst.
Economists said the privatisation proceeds were an important financial injection for the cash-strapped economy which endured four years of sanctions and needs about $1 billion a year to keep going.
